verses.text: But a certain man named Ananias, with Sapphira, his wife, sold a possession,
and kept back part of the price, his wife also being aware of it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles’ feet.
But Peter said, “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart to lie to the Holy Spirit, and to keep back part of the price of the land?
While you kept it, didn’t it remain your own? After it was sold, wasn’t it in your power? How is it that you have conceived this thing in your heart? You haven’t lied to men, but to God.”
Ananias, hearing these words, fell down and died. Great fear came on all who heard these things.
The young men arose and wrapped him up, and they carried him out and buried him.
About three hours later, his wife, not knowing what had happened, came in.
Peter answered her, “Tell me whether you sold the land for so much.” She said, “Yes, for so much.”
But Peter asked her, “How is it that you have agreed together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord? Behold, the feet of those who have buried your husband are at the door, and they will carry you out.”
She fell down immediately at his feet, and died. The young men came in and found her dead, and they carried her out and buried her by her husband.
Great fear came on the whole assembly, and on all who heard these things.
By the hands of the apostles many signs and wonders were done among the people. They were all with one accord in Solomon’s porch.
None of the rest dared to join them, however the people honored them.
More believers were added to the Lord, multitudes of both men and women.
They even carried out the sick into the streets, and laid them on cots and mattresses, so that as Peter came by, at the least his shadow might overshadow some of them.
The multitude also came together from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick people, and those who were tormented by unclean spirits: and they were all healed.
But the high priest rose up, and all those who were with him (which is the sect of the Sadducees), and they were filled with jealousy,
and laid hands on the apostles, and put them in public custody.
But an angel of the Lord opened the prison doors by night, and brought them out, and said,
“Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.”

When they heard this, they entered into the temple about daybreak, and taught. But the high priest came, and those who were with him, and called the council together, and all the senate of the children of Israel, and sent to the prison to have them brought.
But the officers who came didn’t find them in the prison. They returned and reported,
“We found the prison shut and locked, and the guards standing before the doors, but when we opened them, we found no one inside!”
Now when the high priest, the captain of the temple, and the chief priests heard these words, they were very perplexed about them and what might become of this.
One came and told them, “Behold, the men whom you put in prison are in the temple, standing and teaching the people.”
Then the captain went with the officers, and brought them without violence, for they were afraid that the people might stone them.
When they had brought them, they set them before the council. The high priest questioned them,
saying, “Didn’t we strictly command you not to teach in this name? Behold, you have filled Jerusalem with your teaching, and intend to bring this man’s blood on us.”
But Peter and the apostles answered, “We must obey God rather than men.
The God of our fathers raised up Jesus, whom you killed, hanging him on a tree.
God exalted him with his right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel, and remission of sins.
We are His witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey him.”
But they, when they heard this, were cut to the heart, and were determined to kill them.
But one stood up in the council, a Pharisee named Gamaliel, a teacher of the law, honored by all the people, and commanded to put the apostles out for a little while.
He said to them, “You men of Israel, be careful concerning these men, what you are about to do.

For before these days Theudas rose up, making himself out to be somebody; to whom a number of men, about four hundred, joined themselves: who was slain; and all, as many as obeyed him, were dispersed, and came to nothing.
After this man, Judas of Galilee rose up in the days of the enrollment, and drew away some people after him. He also perished, and all, as many as obeyed him, were scattered abroad.
Now I tell you, withdraw from these men, and leave them alone. For if this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown.
But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you would be found even to be fighting against God!”
They agreed with him. Summoning the apostles, they beat them and commanded them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and let them go.
They therefore departed from the presence of the council, rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name.
Every day, in the temple and at home, they never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus, the Christ.

footnotes.content: Ananias and Sapphira seem like any other couple—they own land, they want to give. But here begins one of Scripture's hardest moments: a husband and wife joined in a lie before God. Love should have kept them honest with each other and the Lord.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: That phrase 'his wife also being aware' breaks my heart a little. They conspired together—not forced, not deceived, but complicit. Sometimes the deepest betrayals happen when two people agree to hide from God as one.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter names it plainly: Satan filled Ananias's heart to lie to the Holy Spirit. It's not a gentle rebuke but a wake-up call—a stark choice between the kingdom of darkness and the Spirit's truth. The stakes are higher than money.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter reminds him: the land was yours. You could have given any amount—or none. But you chose to lie, to present yourself as more generous than you were. The Lord isn't after our wealth; He's after our hearts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ananias fell dead. I don't explain why or soften it—the text doesn't. What I see is a community shaken awake to the reality that they live in the presence of the Living God, not in casual religious performance.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The young men wrapped him up and buried him. No panic, no accusation—just immediate, quiet action. The Church knows what it has seen and acts with a kind of solemn courage that comes from standing in the fear of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three hours pass before Sapphira returns, unaware. Those three hours feel like mercy to me—time for the Spirit to prepare her heart, though she doesn't yet know what awaits. Every delay in God's story carries weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter asks her straight: 'Did you sell the land for this price?' She had a choice to break the conspiracy, to confess. Instead she says, 'Yes, for so much'—and with those words seals the course.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter speaks of 'agreeing together to tempt the Spirit of the Lord'—not accidentally stumbling, but deliberately testing God's patience. The feet of those who buried your husband, he says, are at the door. Judgment comes swiftly when we press against the Spirit's knowing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Sapphira falls at his feet and dies the same death. Husband and wife, matched in their deception, matched in their end. They are carried out and buried together. It's the ultimate loneliness—to hide from God with the one you love most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Great fear came on the whole assembly. Not fear of Peter's words, but fear of God's holiness made tangible. In that fear, the early Church learned what it means to live as the body of Christ—serious, awake, stripped of pretense.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The apostles gather in Solomon's porch—the columned walkway on the temple's east side where Jesus Himself once walked and taught. Now His followers stand there, doing signs and wonders, speaking His name in the very place He walked. God doesn't waste sacred ground.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Fear keeps the rest at a distance—not fear of being harmed, but holy awe. The apostles are honored but untouchable, set apart by the Spirit's power. Sometimes the Lord keeps His witnesses distinct so that all eyes turn to Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet believers are added—multitudes of men and women. After Ananias and Sapphira's judgment, the Church grows. It seems backward until you see it: judgment purifies, and a purified witness draws hungry hearts to Jesus.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They brought the sick into the streets on cots and mattresses, hoping Peter's shadow might fall on them. Desperate faith—not sophisticated, but real. They believed that proximity to an apostle meant proximity to healing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: From the cities around Jerusalem they came—sick and tormented by unclean spirits. And they were all healed. The Lord's hand was not shortened; His compassion reached every one. The Kingdom was advancing not through politics but through power and mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high priest and the Sadducees—the very authorities who killed Jesus—rise up filled with jealousy. They see the crowds, the healings, the apostles' boldness, and they recognize a threat to their control. Pride cannot share a room with the Kingdom.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They lay hands on the apostles and put them in public custody—the same machinery that condemned Jesus. But the apostles have learned something: you cannot stop a resurrection people.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An angel of the Lord opens the prison doors by night. Not with drama or explanation, but with quiet authority—the way God works. The imprisoned become liberated; the rulers become powerless.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Go stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life.' Life—not law, not tradition, not our authority, but the living word of Jesus. That's what the angel commands them to proclaim without fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At daybreak the apostles enter the temple and teach. The high priest comes and summons the council—a full assembly to reckon with these fishermen. What neither man knows yet is that obedience to God will outlast every earthly council.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The officers come to the prison and find it locked, the guards standing by. But the apostles are not there. Power meets a greater Power and discovers it has always been on the outside looking in.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'We found the prison shut and locked...but when we opened them, we found no one inside!' The impossibility of it—locked doors, guards, apostles fled. No natural explanation. Just God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The high priest and temple captain hear this and are very perplexed. They wanted to control the narrative, but they can't even find the prisoners. When God moves, human authority becomes confused.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A messenger arrives: 'The men whom you put in prison are in the temple, standing and teaching the people.' Not hiding, not fleeing—teaching openly. Obedience looks like standing in the very place your enemy thought they had secured.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The captain goes with officers to bring the apostles, but without violence—afraid the people might stone them. The authorities have lost moral authority; the apostles have become the people's beloved. Power flows to those who serve, not demand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They set the apostles before the council. Again. The high priest is about to question them as though these are the early rounds of a trial. But in fact, the trial is different than he knows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Didn't we strictly command you not to teach in this name?' The question reveals the council's obsession: not the healings or the signs, but that the name Jesus keeps being spoken. They understand that a name is a power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'We must obey God rather than men.' These words from Peter—once afraid to speak Christ's name, once denying even knowing Him—now speak the defining principle of the Church forever. Fear has been swallowed in faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Peter rehearses it: Jesus was raised by the God of our fathers, whom you killed, hanging Him on a tree. Not to shame them, but to offer them the one mercy they refused: the chance to acknowledge what they did and turn.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: God exalted Him with His right hand to be a Prince and a Savior, to give repentance to Israel. Even now, speaking to the council that condemned Him, Peter offers repentance as the gift. The gospel never stops reaching.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'We are His witnesses of these things; and so also is the Holy Spirit, whom God has given to those who obey Him.' Not a legal testimony but a living one—men and the Spirit Himself testify to Jesus' resurrection and present power.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Hearing this, they were cut to the heart—the same phrase used after Pentecost when people believed. But here it drives them to rage instead of repentance. Hearts can be cut toward Jesus or away from Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Gamaliel stands—a Pharisee, a teacher of the law, honored by all. He commands the apostles to be put out so he can speak. Watch for the quiet sage in the crowd; sometimes God appoints them as hinges for what comes next.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'You men of Israel, be careful concerning these men, what you are about to do.' Gamaliel counsels caution—not faith, but wisdom. Sometimes a voice of reason stays the council's hand long enough for the Spirit's work to spread.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He recalls Theudas, who rose up making himself somebody, and about 400 men followed. But he was slain, and all who obeyed him were dispersed. Gamaliel uses history to make a point: false movements collapse on their own.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After him, Judas of Galilee rose in the days of enrollment and drew people after him. He perished, and those who obeyed him scattered. Again—the pattern of failed rebellions. Gamaliel sees what he wants to see: another movement destined to fade.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Withdraw from these men and leave them alone. If this counsel or this work is of men, it will be overthrown.' He offers a test: time will tell. If it's human, it will fall. If it's of God—well, he hasn't finished that thought.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'But if it is of God, you will not be able to overthrow it, and you would be found fighting against God.' That's the hinge. Gamaliel's caution carries within it a shadow of eternal truth. What if you're wrong about who they serve?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The council agrees, calls the apostles, beats them, and commands them not to speak in Jesus' name, then releases them. Violence, threats, release—the machinery of power grinding away. But it cannot break what belongs to the Spirit.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They departed rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus' name. Readers today hear an echo in these words: that there are things more precious than comfort, that honor in the Lord's eyes outweighs the world's approval. A few of us still understand that.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Every day, in the temple and at home, they never stopped teaching and preaching Jesus, the Christ. Not once. Not when it got hard. Not when they were beaten. Every day—in public and in private—the name Jesus spoken, His love told, His truth proclaimed without end.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
